candidates.title: Which Dwarf Is This? Doppeldwarf-306 and Near-Identical Instance Retrieval
candidates.content: Most established instance-retrieval benchmarks emphasise landmarks; small sculptures from visually similar series offer a complementary challenge. We introduce Doppeldwarf-306: 1,691 openly licensed photographs of 306 bronze dwarf statues in Wrocław, Poland, many made in themed series that share one style, with the photographer of each image recorded. With no training, nearest-neighbour search over frozen DINOv2 features names the right statue first for 93.1% of leave-one-out queries, and the best of thirteen backbones from seven pretraining paradigms reaches 94.7%. Accuracy falls slowly as candidates are added: for DINOv2, by about 0.8 points each time their number doubles. A natural design for a phone guide compares a photograph only with statues near the user. In simulation this helps, but less than an equal number of randomly chosen statues does, so random subsampling overstates its value; a permutation test ties the penalty to the real layout (p = 0.005). Used as a weight instead of a filter, location raises DINOv2 from 93.4% to 98.7% for a simulated user 25 m from the statue. candidates.title: Learning Video Foresight Reasoning from Unlabeled Videos via On-Policy Self-Distillation
candidates.content: Video foresight reasoning requires vision-language models to anticipate future events or next actions from currently observed videos. Existing methods fit future captions, rationales, or full visual states, but face two limitations. First, they rely on annotations or external large models for supervision, limiting scalability. We address this with an on-policy self-distillation framework that turns past-future video pairs into a natural self-supervised signal without extra annotations or LLM supervision. Second, they treat the whole future clip as equally valuable, although most of it is irrelevant context information. We address this by defining a foresight score, from which we obtain a contrastive privilege advantage that drives the model to learn the most valuable future information. Since the score is intractable, we optimize a tractable lower-bound surrogate that interpolates this advantage, computed between the true and a random reference future, with a teacher-student distillation advantage; together, they amplify decision-relevant content information and suppress irrelevant context information. We call the resulting framework Future-OPSD. On open-ended prediction and closed

candidates.title: Taking Apart and Putting Together: Tracking Objects Through Physical Transformations
candidates.content: We introduce Transformation Tracking and Understanding (TTU), extending video object tracking to environments where objects undergo physical assemblies and disassemblies. TTU requires continuously tracking objects through transformations, identifying new entities, maintaining a state graph of their relationships, and assigning semantic labels to transformations. While foundation models (e.g., SAM 2/3) maintain tracklets through appearance changes, they cannot update semantic identities as objects physically evolve. Prior work addresses only disassemblies, relying on expensive searches triggered only when tracking fails. We propose Tracking Instances via Proposals and Overlaps (TIPO), a training-free framework that continuously infers transformations via a generate-evaluate-judge pipeline. TIPO generates split and merge proposals from disjoint mask components, scores them against mask-decoder priors using inner and external overlap, and queries an MLLM on the top proposal for visual verification and semantic labeling. candidates.title: Rapid degradation of six class I HDAC complexes reveals a mixture of unique, cooperative, and antagonistic roles
candidates.content: Abstract The class I histone deacetylases (HDACs) 1, 2, and 3 form seven families of distinct large multiprotein complexes that regulate gene expression via deacetylation of lysines in histone tails. The degree of redundancy and functional overlap between complexes and their acute gene targets remain unknown. We used CRISPR/Cas9 to create six cell lines in which individual HDAC complexes were tagged with FKBP12 F36V enabling rapid (<1 h), PROTAC-mediated, degradation. RNA sequencing at 6 h reveals that together, the four major complexes (CoREST, NuRD, NCoR/SMRT, and SIN3A) perturbed >50% of expressed genes. More than 60% of these are regulated by a single complex. ChIP-sequencing revealed that >54% of differentially expressed genes are directly regulated by the associated complex. Of genes regulated by more than one complex, approaching 50% are reciprocally regulated such that HDAC complexes act as antagonistic regulators. Homer analysis strongly suggests that the complexes are reliant on different transcription factors. candidates.title: Reprogramming mRNA localization by targeted RNA-protein interference reveals roles in oncogenesis
candidates.content: Abstract RNA binding proteins (RBPs) associate with RNAs in intricate ribonucleoprotein complexes and regulate various aspects of RNA life cycle and, by extension, cell functions. Despite their significance, elucidating the functional contributions of specific RNA–RBP binding events, particularly in long-term phenotypic assays, remains challenging. Here, we harness the specificity of CRISPR/dCas13 to interfere with specific RNA–RBP interactions. We apply this methodology to GA-rich mRNA localization elements which recruit the RNA-binding protein CNBP and serve as platforms for the assembly of mRNA trafficking complexes. We show that dCas13/gRNA binds to target transcripts in a highly specific manner and interferes with CNBP recruitment leading to altered target mRNA localization and cell motility, consistent with the function of the targeted mRNAs. We describe optimizations and considerations for the stable implementation of this system. We further use it to show that interfering with the localization of the GA-containing NET1 mRNA reduces cancer cell invasiveness and metastatic lung colonization. candidates.title: Translons upstream of protein-coding regions rather than their products are crucial for proliferation of human cells of distinct origin
candidates.content: Abstract Upstream open reading frames (uORFs) are a widespread class of translated regions (translons) occurring in 5′ leaders of messenger RNAs. They serve critical roles in post-transcriptional regulation and some are known to encode small proteins and peptideins. Yet it is not known which of these modes of function is more critical for human cells. We conducted a CRISPR-Cas9 mutagenesis screening targeting 969 translated human uORFs across three cell lines of distinct origin. Disruption of 155 uORFs impaired cell proliferation, although these effects were highly cell-type specific, with only six shared across all cell lines. Neither evolutionary conservation, comparative protein-coding potential, nor population mutational constraint distinguished uORF hits. Instead, high-throughput analysis of CRISPR-induced mutations combined with reporter assays demonstrated that proliferation phenotypes arise from altered cis -regulation of coding sequence (CDS) translation. candidates.title: AutoOntologyBench: A Task-Grounded Benchmark for Agentic Knowledge Engineering
candidates.content: arXiv:2611.27734v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Foundation-model agents are increasingly extending beyond software engineering (SWE) into autonomous scientific research, where acquiring and integrating domain knowledge remains a critical challenge. Recent industrial advances have increasingly adopted knowledge graphs and ontology-based semantic layers to organize heterogeneous knowledge into reusable representations. We ask: Can autonomous agents construct ontologies that help them solve real tasks, and do they offer measurable benefits over alternative knowledge representations? Existing benchmarks evaluate ontology correctness or agent task success in isolation, leaving the value of autonomously acquired knowledge unresolved. We therefore introduce AutoOntologyBench, a task-grounded benchmark comprising 19,947 audited tasks grounded in 18 real-world knowledge sources across 7 domains, with source-native verification. Spanning Application, Repair, Organization, and Construction, AutoOntologyBench compares nine frontier-model agents under matched knowledge representations. candidates.title: From Novel Combinations to Informative Absence: Structural permission, communicative opportunity, and form choice in language learning
candidates.content: arXiv:2611.27762v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Language learners must infer which novel expressions are grammatically licensed and when continued absence is evidence against them. Our generative theory unites these capacities via counterfactual expression opportunities, decomposing utterance generation into structural permission, communicative opportunity, and form choice. First, shared predictive continuations recover structural permission for unseen word-construction pairings across 30 artificial grammars (mean AUC 0.945 after 120 sentences). Second, under hierarchical uncertainty, we derive a joint evidence law linking omissions to context diversity and within-context repetition, and an exact finite-sample context-refinement inequality. Thus, observing related expressions calibrates expected use to sharpen negative evidence, and higher expected use can drive steeper posterior declines for stronger-permission candidates (reversing initial order after six omissions in a fixed-rate example).
